title: Symptom Spotter: name the phenomenon
hook: Read what a patient says, in their own words, and name the descriptive phenomenon, telling it apart from the…
objective: Read what a patient says, in their own words, and name the descriptive phenomenon, telling it apart from the classic look-alikes (delusion vs overvalued idea vs obsession; hallucination vs pseudohallucination vs illusion; insertion vs obsessional intrusion; derailment vs tangentiality vs circumstantiality; depersonalisation vs derealisation).

categories.label: Passivity / made experience (act, feeling, impulse, somatic)

items.quote: Every night two men stand outside my window and talk about me: 'he's useless, he'll fail again.' I hear them as clearly as I hear you, but my wife says the lane is empty.
items.explain: No real sound is being misheard (so not an illusion), and the voices are out in the world and taken as real, not inside the head with insight (so not a pseudohallucination). Voices discussing the patient in the third person are also a first-rank form.

items.quote: A man's voice from near the ceiling fan tells me to go up to the terrace and stand on the edge to prove I'm not a coward. The fan is switched off when he speaks.
items.explain: A command (imperative) hallucination: a voice heard from outside, with no stimulus. An obsessional harm thought would be recognised as the patient's own thought and resisted, not heard as someone else's voice.

items.quote: There is a smell of burning rubber in my room all the time. I can smell it right now, even though my mother sniffs the air and says there is nothing.
items.explain: The patient actually smells the odour, with no source. If they only believed they smelled bad because people wrinkle their noses, without smelling anything, that would be a delusion. A persistent olfactory hallucination should make you think of an organic cause.

items.quote: I can feel tiny insects crawling under the skin of my arms. I feel their legs moving. I've scratched until it bled.
items.explain: Tactile hallucination of small creatures crawling (formication), typical of acute organic states and stimulant (cocaine) psychosis. There is a definite sensation with no stimulus; it is not a belief without a sensation.

items.quote: Since my father died I hear his voice inside my head saying 'eat properly, beta.' It isn't in the room. It's in my mind and I know it's my own memory talking, but I can't switch it off.
items.explain: The voice is in inner, subjective space, it comes on its own, and insight is kept, so on Jaspers' criteria it is a pseudohallucination. It is not an obsession because it is not a senseless thought that the person fights. In grief this can be within normal experience.

items.quote: At night a soft voice inside my head, not in my ears, comments on what I'm doing. I know nobody is really speaking, yet it isn't me choosing to think it.
items.explain: It is involuntary and located inside the head, with insight, so it is a pseudohallucination. It is not thought echo, because the voice is not repeating the person's own thoughts, and not insertion, because no alien thoughts are being placed in the mind. The concept is contested: Hare defined it by insight, which fluctuates.

items.quote: In the dim ward at night, the drip stand next to my bed became a man standing over me with a lathi. When the sister switched the light on, it was only the stand.
items.explain: A real object (the stand) was misperceived and merged into a new perception, which is an illusion. It is common when attention is poor and the person is frightened, as in delirium. A hallucination would need no stimulus at all.

items.quote: Two weeks after my brother's accident I saw his face in the crowd at Dadar station for a second. Then it was a stranger's face.
items.explain: An affect illusion: a real face, distorted for a moment by grief and expectation, then corrected. It is common in bereavement and is not in itself a sign of illness.

items.quote: Whenever the fan is running I hear its hum, and with it, separately, a woman's voice calling me a sinner. When the fan stops, she stops too.
items.explain: The stimulus (the hum) and the voice are heard at the same time and as separate things, which is a functional hallucination. In an illusion the hum itself would turn into the words.

items.quote: Each time the pressure cooker whistles I hear a man saying my name over it. I hear both together, the whistle and his voice, very clearly.
items.explain: The voice needs the whistle to appear, but the whistle is still heard as a whistle. Both exist side by side, so this is functional, not an illusion (which transforms the stimulus).

items.quote: Where do I live? Malad. Mall, I love malls, shopping, shopping for shoes, shoes for cricket, cricket, wicket, ticket, I'll buy you a ticket doctor, let's fly!
items.explain: The thoughts come fast and each jump can be followed (rhyme, sound, chance association), so this is flight of ideas, typical of mania. In derailment you cannot work out the link between one idea and the next.

items.quote: I've got a hundred plans: the app, the dhaba franchise. Franchise, France, I'll learn French. Paris, the Eiffel Tower is iron, iron tablets, my mother needs iron tablets, I'll start a pharmacy!
items.explain: There is pressure, and each link is understandable (verbal and chance associations), but the speaker never gets back to a goal. Tangentiality has no pressure or clanging, and circumstantiality does reach its point.

title: Then and now: is this still the law?
hook: Spot outdated legal content in older teaching notes.
objective: Spot outdated legal content in older teaching notes. Decide whether each statement is still current, updated (same principle, new statute or section), or replaced, and give the current position.

categories.label: Updated (same rule, new statute or section)

items.text: Involuntary 'admission under special circumstances' at a relative's request, for up to 90 days, under the Mental Health Act 1987.
items.explain: The MHA 1987 was repealed by the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (in force 29 May 2018). Supported admission now lasts up to 30 days (s.89), and longer stays need Mental Health Review Board oversight (s.90).

items.text: Admission categories: voluntary, special circumstances, reception order on application, reception order without application before a Magistrate, judicial inquisition, mentally ill prisoner.
items.explain: Under the MHCA 2017 the categories are independent admission, supported admission (up to 30 days and beyond 30 days), minors' admission and emergency treatment (72 hours). There is a separate route for prisoners (s.103).

items.text: The 'mentally ill person' is someone needing treatment for any mental disorder other than mental retardation.
items.explain: MHCA 2017 s.2(1)(s) defines mental illness functionally: a substantial disorder of thinking, mood, perception, orientation or memory that grossly impairs judgement, behaviour, the capacity to recognise reality or the ability to meet ordinary demands of life. 'Mental retardation' is now intellectual disability (RPwD Act 2016).

items.text: Criminal responsibility: IPC Section 84 (a McNaughten-type test of unsoundness of mind).
items.explain: The same test continues as Section 22 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (in force 1 July 2024). The wording is the same; only the section number has changed.

items.text: Attempted suicide is punishable under IPC Section 309.
items.explain: MHCA 2017 s.115 presumes severe stress and says the person shall not be tried or punished, and the government must provide care. The BNS 2023 has no general offence of attempting suicide (a narrower provision about attempts to compel a public servant is a separate issue).

items.text: A 'lunatic' may be incompetent as a witness under the Indian Evidence Act 1872, Section 118.
items.explain: The Indian Evidence Act has been replaced by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (in force 1 July 2024). The competency principle is kept, under a new section number.

items.text: Testamentary capacity: a will requires a 'sound and disposing mind' (Indian Succession Act 1925, s.59).
items.explain: Still the governing law. The capacity tests (nature of the act, extent of the property, who has claims) remain standard practice.

items.text: Contract: a person must be of sound mind to contract (Indian Contract Act 1872, s.11).
items.explain: Still in force.

items.text: Hindu Marriage Act: unsoundness of mind, mental disorder or 'recurrent attacks of insanity or epilepsy' make a marriage voidable; incurable unsoundness is a divorce ground.
items.explain: Mental disorder grounds remain, but 'epilepsy' was removed from s.5(ii)(c) by amendment (1999). Courts now read 'unsound mind' narrowly and look at function. Never treat a diagnosis alone as grounds.

items.text: Rights of patients (MHA 1987, Chapter VIII): no indignity or cruelty, research only with consent, no interception of letters.
items.explain: MHCA 2017 Chapter V sets out a much wider list of rights: access to mental healthcare, community living, protection from cruel treatment, equality, information, confidentiality, access to records, legal aid and complaints. It also adds advance directives and nominated representatives.

items.text: Direct (unmodified) ECT is described as a technique in use.
items.explain: MHCA 2017 s.95 prohibits ECT without muscle relaxants and anaesthesia, and restricts ECT in minors.

items.text: Research ethics: ICMR Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research on Human Subjects, 2000.
items.explain: Replaced by the ICMR National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, 2017.

title: Culture or symptom?
hook: Tell culturally shared beliefs and idioms apart from cultural distress syndromes, dissociative possession,…
objective: Tell culturally shared beliefs and idioms apart from cultural distress syndromes, dissociative possession, and psychotic phenomena in the Indian setting.

items.quote: For three months I've felt weak and dizzy because dhat is passing in my urine. My body's strength is going.
items.explain: Dhat: a culturally shaped distress syndrome (weakness and fatigue blamed on semen loss), often with depression or anxiety underneath. It is not a delusion.

items.quote: My penis is shrinking into my belly and when it disappears I'll die. Please help, hold it!
items.explain: Koro: acute fear of the genitals retracting, which can spread in epidemics. It is usually an acute anxiety state, not a fixed delusion, but rule out psychosis if it persists.

items.quote: (Family report) At the temple fair she began swaying, spoke in a deep voice as the Devi, and gave orders. An hour later she was herself again and remembered nothing.
items.explain: Episodic trance or possession, with a change of identity and amnesia afterwards, and a return to normal. Decide whether it is a culturally sanctioned ritual (normal) or causes distress and dysfunction (a disorder).

items.quote: We tie a black thread on the baby's wrist so no one's evil eye harms her. My whole family does this.
items.explain: A belief shared by the patient's culture and family is not a delusion by definition, because a delusion must be out of keeping with the person's background.

items.quote: My neighbour has done black magic on me. She puts the spells into my head through the wall at night, and I hear her laughing from inside the cupboard.
items.explain: Belief in black magic can be cultural, but here it comes with thought insertion and hallucinations, it is personal and fixed, and the family does not share it. Look at the form (insertion, voices), not just the cultural content.
items.ref: Fish Ch 3, p.38 (PDF 42); Ahuja Ch 2, p.13 (PDF 25)

items.quote: Since the exam results, a spirit comes over me in the evenings. I shake and fall. My parents say it's the ancestor; I'm scared it'll happen in front of my in-laws.
items.explain: Possession-type dissociative episodes linked to stress. Check for epilepsy and look at the psychosocial stressors.

items.quote: I am the Devi herself. I was born to destroy this world's sinners, and I've stopped eating because gods don't need food.
items.explain: Here the person continuously and fully believes they are the deity (a grandiose delusion), with no episodic trance and no return to their usual self. That is psychotic, not possession trance. In possession the person is usually aware of the 'possessor' as someone else.
items.ref: Ahuja Ch 8, p.102 (PDF 114); Fish Ch 3, p.43 (PDF 47)

items.quote: My son's weakness is from too much 'heat' in his body. We've stopped giving him mangoes and eggs.
items.explain: Hot/cold humoral explanations are a shared explanatory model. Record them, respect them, and negotiate treatment within them.

title: Red-flag triage: how fast does this need a doctor?
hook: Given a short account from a client or family member who is taking psychiatric medicine, decide how quickly…
objective: Given a short account from a client or family member who is taking psychiatric medicine, decide how quickly a medical professional must see them (routine, discuss with the prescriber soon, or urgent same-day medical review), name the cues that drove the decision, and state the psychologist's next action without giving medical advice.

items.vignette: Imran's sister calls before his session. Imran, 24, has schizophrenia and his antipsychotic was increased last week. Since yesterday he has been very stiff, sweating heavily, feels hot to touch and is not making sense. He was talking normally three days ago.
items.explain: Stiffness, fever, sweating and a change in consciousness soon after an antipsychotic change is the classic pattern of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. It is rare (estimated incidence 0.11-0.16%), but it can be fatal. Recent or rapid dose increase and dehydration are listed risk factors. This needs emergency medical care today, not a therapy session. Your move: Advise the family to take him to an emergency department now (or call an ambulance), and tell them to bring his medicine list. Inform the prescriber and the team. Document.

items.vignette: Kavita, 38, takes an SSRI for depression. Two days ago another doctor added a medicine for her migraines. Today in session she is shaky and restless, has jerky leg movements, is sweating, says her heart is racing and has had diarrhoea since morning. Her pupils look large.
items.explain: This picture fits serotonin syndrome, which is more likely when two serotonergic medicines are combined. Agitation, myoclonus, tremor, dilated pupils and sweating fall in the moderate band of the usual severity scale. Severe cases can progress to high fever, rigidity and confusion. Moderate features already need same-day medical assessment. Your move: Stop the session, explain calmly that this may be a medicine reaction that needs a doctor today, and arrange urgent medical review (emergency department if symptoms are worsening). Tell the team about both prescribers.

items.vignette: Arun, 34, started an SSRI five days ago. He says he has felt a little queasy after the morning tablet and slightly jittery, but both are already easing. No fever, no shaking, no diarrhoea. His mood is unchanged and he has no thoughts of self-harm.
items.explain: Mild nausea and some jitteriness are common in the first days of an SSRI and often settle. Nothing here suggests serotonin syndrome (no tremor, jerks, sweating or fever). This is a good moment for psychoeducation: early side effects often come before benefit, which can take weeks. Your move: Normalise, encourage him to mention it at his planned review, and tell him what would need faster contact (worsening restlessness, shaking, fever, or any thoughts of self-harm). Keep screening risk at each session.

items.vignette: Mrs Fernandes, 61, has taken lithium for bipolar disorder for many years. Three weeks ago her GP started a 'water tablet' for blood pressure. She now has a coarse tremor, has been vomiting, walks unsteadily and seems muddled on the phone.
items.explain: Diuretics, especially thiazides, reduce lithium clearance, and levels usually rise within 10 days of a thiazide being started. GI upset with coarse tremor, unsteadiness and confusion is the typical picture of lithium toxicity. It can progress to seizures and coma. Your move: Same-day emergency medical assessment. Tell the family to bring all her medicines, including the new tablet. Inform the psychiatrist and the GP.

items.vignette: Dev, 45, has been well on lithium for six years. He mentions in passing that his hands have always had a slight fine shake when he holds a cup. It has not changed, the team knows about it, and he has no other symptoms.
items.explain: A fine tremor is a recognised common side effect of lithium. What matters is change: a tremor that becomes coarse, or comes with vomiting, unsteadiness or confusion, is a toxicity warning. Your move: Note it. Remind him what change would be a warning sign. He can raise it at routine monitoring.

items.vignette: Salma, 29, is well on lithium. She tells you she plans to start a strict low-salt diet to lose weight and will also be fasting through long, hot summer days next month. She has not told her psychiatrist.
items.explain: Most risk factors for lithium toxicity involve sodium or fluid balance, for example low-salt diets and dehydration. Nothing is wrong yet, but the plan changes her risk. The prescriber should know before she starts so that monitoring can be adjusted. Your move: Explain the link without alarm, support her to contact her psychiatrist before starting, and agree that she will tell you if she feels unwell. Respect the reasons behind the fast and the diet. Do not argue her out of them.

items.vignette: Tarun, 52, on lithium, says that over the past few months he is always thirsty and gets up three or four times a night to pass urine. He otherwise feels fine and his mood is stable.
items.explain: Thirst and passing a lot of urine are known lithium effects on the kidney. Long-term kidney function is monitored on lithium. This is not an emergency, but it should be reported, not just put up with. Drinking less to avoid night-time trips could make dehydration and toxicity more likely. Your move: Encourage him to tell the prescriber this week and to keep drinking normally. Escalate to urgent if vomiting, unsteadiness or confusion appear.

items.vignette: Ramesh, 31, started clozapine six weeks ago. His mother says he has had a sore throat and fever since last night and now has painful mouth ulcers. He is tired but talking normally.
items.explain: Any sign of infection on clozapine (fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, flu-like illness) must be checked the same day for a dangerously low white cell count. Agranulocytosis affects about 0.4% of clozapine patients. The risk is highest early and falls after the first year. The team will arrange an urgent blood count. Your move: Contact the clozapine team or prescriber today and make sure he is seen for a blood test today. Do not wait for the next routine blood test.

items.vignette: Joseph, 40, has been on clozapine for two years. In session he looks uncomfortable and holds his stomach. He has not opened his bowels for five days, feels bloated, and vomited this morning. He thought it was 'just gas'.
items.explain: Clozapine slows the gut. Constipation affects more than 30% of patients, and when it is severe the case fatality is around 20-30%. It can happen at any time in treatment. Vomiting and pain with no bowel opening suggest possible obstruction, which is an emergency. Your move: Same-day medical assessment (emergency department if pain is severe). Tell the team. Afterwards, add bowel habit to your routine check-in questions with him.

items.vignette: Faisal, 36, on clozapine for a year, stopped smoking ten days ago after a chest infection scare. Proud of himself, he mentions that he is now sleeping most of the day, feels very groggy and had 'a few sudden jerks' in his arms yesterday.
items.explain: Smoking speeds up the liver enzyme (CYP1A2) that clears clozapine, so smoking can reduce clozapine levels by up to 50%. After stopping, enzyme activity roughly halves every 2 days, so levels can rise sharply. Nicotine replacement does not prevent this. Heavy sedation and jerks suggest the level may now be too high. Your move: Arrange same-day medical review and tell the prescriber he has stopped smoking. Praise the quit attempt. The problem is the unplanned change, not the quitting.

items.vignette: Neha, 27, on clozapine, has been working with you on motivation and tells you she has set a date to quit smoking next month. She feels well.
items.explain: Quitting is a good health goal, and the prescriber needs to plan for it because clozapine levels rise when smoking stops. Informing the team before the quit date lets them plan monitoring. Your move: Support the quit plan, and help her tell the prescriber before the quit date. Agree to watch for sleepiness or jerks after she stops.

items.vignette: Vikram, 23, started clozapine three weeks ago. He says he has had a 'flu' for two days with fever, feels his heart pounding even at rest, gets breathless on the stairs and had chest pain this morning.
items.explain: Myocarditis, an inflammation of the heart muscle, is a known clozapine risk. It is most likely in the first 6-8 weeks (median 3 weeks) and is potentially fatal. Symptoms include fever, flu-like illness, a fast heart rate, breathlessness and chest pain. Your move: Emergency medical assessment now; chest pain with breathlessness means calling emergency services. Inform the clozapine team.

debrief: Pattern to remember: (1) Unwell body plus psychiatric medicine (fever, rigidity, confusion, vomiting, chest pain, rash with fever, infection on clozapine, no bowel movement on clozapine) means same day. (2) A change that raises risk but no symptoms yet (planned quit smoking, low-salt diet, pregnancy, missed doses) means tell the prescriber soon, before the change. (3) Known, stable, mild effects mean routine, as long as you have said what would make it faster.

title: Four look-alike emergencies
hook: Distinguish neuroleptic malignant syndrome, serotonin syndrome, lithium toxicity and anticholinergic…
objective: Distinguish neuroleptic malignant syndrome, serotonin syndrome, lithium toxicity and anticholinergic toxicity by medicine history, speed of onset and key signs, while recognising that all four need same-day medical care.

items.vignette: Day 3 after a second serotonergic medicine was added: anxious, sweating, jerking legs, diarrhoea.
items.explain: Fast onset after a serotonergic combination; jerks and diarrhoea.

items.vignette: Gradual over several days after an antipsychotic increase: stiff as a board, hot, sweating, drifting in and out.
items.explain: Rigidity, fever and fluctuating consciousness after an antipsychotic change.

items.vignette: Long-term mood-stabiliser user after a week of diarrhoea in a heatwave: vomiting, big shaky tremor, staggering, muddled.
items.explain: Fluid loss is a key trigger; GI plus coarse tremor plus ataxia plus confusion.

items.vignette: Older man on several medicines including one for bladder spasm and an old-style antidepressant: dry mouth, hot dry skin, cannot pass urine, confused and picking at the air.
items.explain: Dry, hot skin and urinary retention with confusion: muscarinic blockade.

debrief: You do not need to settle the label. Every one of these is 'unwell and on medicine': same-day medical care. Getting the likely label right helps you tell the doctor what changed.

title: Akathisia or anxiety?
hook: Tell drug-induced akathisia apart from anxiety, psychotic agitation and restless legs by timing, the inner…
objective: Tell drug-induced akathisia apart from anxiety, psychotic agitation and restless legs by timing, the inner urge to move, the movement pattern and context, and explain why the distinction matters for risk and for the therapeutic relationship.

items.vignette: Two weeks after a new antipsychotic, Deepak keeps standing up mid-sentence. 'It's not worry. My legs just won't let me stay still.' Breathing exercises make no difference.
items.explain: Timing, an urge to move without fear content, no response to relaxation.

items.vignette: Before an exam, Nisha fidgets and jiggles her foot, her heart races, and she fears she will fail. On no medicine.
items.explain: Fear content, situational trigger, no medicine change.

items.vignette: Harish paces, shouting that the neighbours are sending signals through the wall; this began before any treatment.
items.explain: Restlessness driven by psychotic content, predating medicine.

items.vignette: Priya says she 'can't settle' in the evenings. You do not know her medicines or when it began.
items.explain: Timing relative to medicine changes is the key question.

items.vignette: A week after his antipsychotic dose went up, Kiran says, 'I'm crawling out of my skin; I can't take this,' and rocks from foot to foot when standing.
items.explain: Recent increase, inner unease, classic rocking. Assess risk because distress is high.

debrief: Mislabelled akathisia can be read as 'non-engagement' or 'worsening psychosis'. A link with suicidal ideation has been suggested. Naming it as a likely side effect, and passing that to the prescriber, protects the client and the alliance.

title: "I've stopped my lithium": an adherence conversation
hook: Respond to a client who has stopped a mood stabiliser by exploring their reasons, beliefs and values before…
objective: Respond to a client who has stopped a mood stabiliser by exploring their reasons, beliefs and values before giving information. Respect their autonomy, check safety, and agree a next step that keeps the prescriber involved.

items.prompt: Raghav, 29, software tester, bipolar I disorder, well for 18 months on lithium. He arrives saying: 'I stopped my lithium three weeks ago. I feel flat on it and I'm tired of blood tests. I'm fine now, so I don't need it.'

responses.text: You've made a big decision. Can you tell me what made you decide, and what it has been like since?
responses.why: Opens with curiosity. People stop for reasons, and knowing them is the starting point.

responses.text: Stopping lithium is risky. You need to restart it.
responses.why: Persuading before understanding usually increases resistance.
Important later, but as an opener it can feel like checking up on him.

items.prompt: “Feeling flat is the worst part. I used to be the funny one. And the blood tests make me feel like a patient forever.”

responses.text: So the medicine has cost you something that matters (feeling like yourself) and the tests are a reminder of the illness.
responses.why: Reflects both meaning and loss. He feels heard.

responses.text: Lots of people feel flat; you get used to it.
Flatness can sometimes be adjusted. Your psychiatrist could look at that.
responses.why: True and useful, but offered before he has finished telling his story.

responses.text: Since stopping, have you noticed any changes in sleep, energy, spending or how fast your thoughts go?
responses.why: Checks for early relapse signs without lecturing. Abrupt stopping of psychotropics worsens outcomes, so early warning signs matter.
A frightening prediction that damages trust.

responses.text: Let's not talk about the medicine today.
Would it be OK if I shared what I know about stopping lithium, and you tell me what fits for you?
responses.why: Asking permission keeps him in charge of the decision.

responses.text: Here are the statistics on relapse after stopping.
responses.why: Information without permission can feel like a lecture.

responses.text: It's your choice, so I won't say anything.
responses.why: Respecting autonomy does not mean withholding relevant information.

responses.text: Whatever you decide, would you be willing to see your psychiatrist this week so the decision is made with full information, and we agree on signs that would mean getting help early?
responses.why: Keeps the prescriber involved, builds a relapse-signature plan, and respects his choice. NICE guidance says a capacitous person's right to decline should be respected, with concerns recorded.

responses.text: I'll call your psychiatrist and tell them you're non-compliant.
responses.why: Labels and bypasses him; consent and confidentiality rules apply.

responses.text: Just restart at your old dose tonight.
responses.why: Dosing advice is outside a psychologist's role.

title: Clozapine year one: what the psychologist watches
hook: Across one year of a client's clozapine treatment, recognise the side effects and life changes that need…
objective: Across one year of a client's clozapine treatment, recognise the side effects and life changes that need action (infection signs, chest symptoms, constipation, hypersalivation, smoking change, metabolic change) and choose the right speed of escalation, while supporting the client's recovery goals.

nodes.text: Suresh, 27, treatment-resistant schizophrenia, lives with his parents in Nagpur, wants to return to his job at a print shop. Starts clozapine in hospital, then continues at home. Week 3: Suresh says he has had a fever and feels his heart racing even sitting still. He is breathless climbing the stairs.

choices.text: Arrange urgent same-day medical review and alert the team
choices.feedback: He is checked for myocarditis, which is most likely in the first 6-8 weeks.

choices.text: Suggest rest and fluids for the 'flu'
choices.feedback: Heart inflammation can be fatal.

choices.text: Mention it at next week's session
choices.feedback: Too slow for chest symptoms in early clozapine treatment.

nodes.text: Month 2: He is calmer and the voices are quieter. His mother mentions he hardly goes to the toilet and complains of a 'heavy stomach'.

choices.text: Tell the team today and ask Suresh directly about bowel habits from now on
choices.feedback: Constipation is common and can be deadly; active questioning is advised.

choices.text: Suggest more vegetables and leave it
choices.feedback: Diet helps prevention, but the team needs to know now.

choices.text: Assume it's from inactivity
choices.feedback: Missed hypomotility has a high case fatality.

nodes.text: Month 4: He is embarrassed about drooling at night and has skipped some evening doses.

choices.text: Normalise it, and help him tell the prescriber this week, including the missed doses
choices.feedback: Hypersalivation is manageable. Restarting after gaps needs medical advice.

choices.text: Tell him to just take the morning dose
choices.feedback: Dose decisions belong to the prescriber.

choices.text: Ignore it; it's cosmetic
choices.feedback: It is driving non-adherence.

nodes.text: Month 6: Motivated by your work together, he wants to quit smoking next month.

choices.text: Support the plan and help him inform the prescriber before the quit date
choices.feedback: Stopping smoking can raise clozapine levels sharply; smoking can cut levels by up to 50%.

choices.text: Advise him not to quit while on clozapine
choices.feedback: Quitting is a health goal; it just needs planning.

choices.text: Suggest nicotine patches so levels stay the same
choices.feedback: Nicotine replacement does not prevent the change; it is the smoke, not nicotine, that speeds up the enzyme.

nodes.text: Month 9: He has gained weight and feels ashamed at the gym. He asks whether he should stop the 'fattening tablet'.

choices.text: Explore the impact, link him with the team's physical-health monitoring, and start behavioural work on activity and eating that he chooses
choices.feedback: Metabolic effects are common with several antipsychotics and need monitoring; behaviour change is the psychologist's strength.

choices.text: Tell him weight gain is the price of recovery
choices.feedback: Dismissive; weight gain is a common reason people stop treatment.

choices.text: Agree he should stop
choices.feedback: Outside your role; abrupt stopping risks relapse.

nodes.text: Month 11: He has a sore throat and fever the week before his job interview.

choices.text: Same-day contact with the clozapine team for a blood count
choices.feedback: Any infection sign on clozapine needs a same-day white cell check.

choices.text: Treat it as a cold; the high-risk period is over
choices.feedback: Risk is much lower after year one but not zero; checking is still the rule.

title: Interaction families
hook: Match common real-life situations to the interaction family they belong to, and to the psychologist's…
objective: Match common real-life situations to the interaction family they belong to, and to the psychologist's response, without learning drug-by-drug tables.

items.text: A client on lithium starts over-the-counter painkillers for back pain.
items.explain: Tell the prescriber; some painkillers (NSAIDs) can raise lithium.

items.text: A client on clozapine is admitted to a no-smoking ward.
items.explain: Make sure the team knows smoking status changed.

items.text: A client on an SSRI is prescribed a strong painkiller by a dentist that also acts on serotonin.
items.explain: Suggest they tell both prescribers what they take; know serotonin syndrome warning signs.

items.text: A client on a benzodiazepine says he drinks most nights to 'switch off'.
items.explain: Explore drinking, screen risk, and share with the prescriber with consent.

items.text: A client's epilepsy medicine was changed, and since then her antidepressant 'stopped working'.
items.explain: Suggest she ask her doctors whether the new medicine affects the other; some anticonvulsants, such as carbamazepine, speed up liver enzymes.

items.text: A client using MDMA at weekends is also on an SSRI.
items.explain: Non-judgemental harm-reduction conversation; inform prescriber with consent (serotonin syndrome risk).

items.text: A client on lithium has been vomiting with a stomach bug for two days.
items.explain: Same-day medical review: fluid loss raises lithium.

debrief: You do not need to know every interaction. Ask about every medicine, supplement, substance and smoking change, and tell the prescriber when something changes.

title: "Nothing works": checking before calling it resistant
hook: Before accepting that a client's illness is 'treatment-resistant', identify the factors a psychologist can…
objective: Before accepting that a client's illness is 'treatment-resistant', identify the factors a psychologist can check and contribute (diagnosis, adherence, substances, psychological treatment dose, physical illness, ongoing stressors), and describe treatment resistance as a concept without recommending medicines.

nodes.text: Meenal, 44, school administrator, depressed for two years. She says, 'I've tried three tablets. Nothing works. I'm a hopeless case.' Where do you start?

choices.text: Map her treatment story: what was tried, for how long, and how she actually took it
choices.feedback: Adequacy and adherence are the first checks; partial adherence is common and often hidden.

choices.text: Agree she is treatment-resistant and focus on acceptance
choices.feedback: Premature, and it reinforces hopelessness.

choices.text: Suggest she asks for ECT
choices.feedback: Treatment choice is not the psychologist's call and is premature.

nodes.text: She admits she often stopped each tablet after 10 days because of nausea.

choices.text: Reflect that these may not have been full trials, and help her share this openly with her psychiatrist
choices.feedback: Pseudo-resistance: short or partial trials are not true failures.

choices.text: Tell her she sabotaged her treatment
choices.feedback: Shaming reduces honesty.

nodes.text: Screening reveals nightly drinking since her divorce and untreated hypothyroidism symptoms.

choices.text: Address drinking collaboratively and encourage a medical check of physical causes; share both with the team with consent
choices.feedback: Substance use and physical illness are classic contributors to apparent resistance.

choices.text: Focus only on mood
choices.feedback: Misses modifiable factors.

nodes.text: She has never had a structured psychological therapy.

choices.text: Offer an evidence-based therapy at a full dose of sessions as part of the plan
choices.feedback: Combined treatment is the norm; therapy 'dose' matters as much as drug dose.

choices.text: Wait until the medicine works
choices.feedback: Delays an effective treatment.

debrief: Treatment resistance is a concept for when adequate, properly taken treatments have not helped. The prescriber decides on medical next steps (for schizophrenia, clozapine is an option for refractory illness). The psychologist's role is to make sure the 'adequate and properly taken' parts are true, and to keep hope realistic.

title: The alcohol withdrawal clock
hook: Place alcohol withdrawal features on a timeline from the last drink so that dangerous stages are anticipated.
objective: Place alcohol withdrawal features on a timeline from the last drink so that dangerous stages are anticipated. Mr. Sukhwinder, 46, a truck driver, is admitted for a leg fracture at 10 pm. His wife says his last drink was at 6 pm.

events.text: Tremulousness (shaky hands), with irritability, sweating and nausea
Perceptual disturbances (for example fleeting visual or tactile misperceptions)
Delirium tremens: confusion, hallucinations, autonomic instability

debrief: Timings are typical, not fixed. Use a structured withdrawal scale and give thiamine before glucose.

title: How a gambling problem unfolds
hook: Order the classic four-phase description of gambling disorder and recognise each phase in a story.
objective: Order the classic four-phase description of gambling disorder and recognise each phase in a story.

events.text: Vikram, 24, wins a large sum on a fantasy-cricket app in his first month and tells friends he has 'a system'.
He starts planning his day around matches, borrows from his cousin and takes bigger risks to win back losses.
He takes loans from several instant-loan apps, misses repayments and secretly pawns his mother's gold bangle.
He accepts the money is gone for good but keeps betting for the thrill, and says he feels nothing else is worth doing.

debrief: This four-phase description is a classic clinical model, not a law. The full course can take many years. Ask about suicidal thoughts in the desperate and hopeless phases.

title: Which test answers the question?
hook: Match commonly used psychological and neuropsychological tests to what they mainly assess.
objective: Match commonly used psychological and neuropsychological tests to what they mainly assess.

pairs.right: Overall intellectual functioning, reported as a range rather than one exact number
Simple attention span, and mentally manipulating information
Attention, speed and switching between two sequences
Working out a rule and shifting when it changes (perseverative errors)
Objective, self-report personality and psychopathology profile with validity scales
Projective test: responses to ambiguous inkblots
Projective test: stories told about ambiguous picture cards

title: How a fear is learned, and unlearned
hook: Apply classical conditioning terms to a clinical phobia, and understand extinction as new learning that can…
objective: Apply classical conditioning terms to a clinical phobia, and understand extinction as new learning that can be reversed. Meera, 16, was trapped in a lift in her apartment block during a power cut and was terrified in the dark for 40 minutes. Afterwards, the sound of the lift doors closing made her heart race, so she took the stairs to the 9th floor every day. With her therapist she rode the lift again and again, starting with one floor. After weeks of this the fear faded. A year later she got stuck briefly in a mall lift during a power failure, and her old fear came back.

pairs.right: Being trapped in the dark (frightening in itself)
The sound of lift doors closing
Racing heart when the doors close

pairs.left: Avoidance that keeps the fear going

pairs.right: Repeated lift rides with nothing bad happening
Fear returning after getting stuck in the mall lift

debrief: Extinction does not erase the original learning. It adds a competing memory, and context or a new frightening event can bring the fear back. This is why relapse prevention plans exposure in different settings.

title: Breaking bad news: the first two minutes
hook: Choose responses that prepare, check what the person wants to know, use plain language and promise continued…
objective: Choose responses that prepare, check what the person wants to know, use plain language and promise continued care.

items.prompt: You are a psychology trainee in the oncology liaison team. The oncologist has told Mr Iqbal, 49, that his cancer has spread. Afterwards, sitting with you in a quiet room, he says: “They used a lot of words I didn't follow. Just tell me straight, how long do I have?”

responses.text: Doctors usually say six months to a year for this stage.
responses.why: Gives a survival estimate that is usually inaccurate, outside your role, and without checking understanding.

responses.text: Don't think about that now. Stay positive and everything will be fine.
responses.why: False reassurance closes the conversation and abandons his question.

responses.text: That's a very hard question, and I can hear you want honesty. Can you tell me what you understood from the doctor, and how much detail you'd like right now? I'll make sure you get clear answers from your oncologist, and I'll stay with you through this.
responses.why: Acknowledges feeling, checks understanding and how much he wants to know, offers plain information through the right person, and promises non-abandonment.

responses.text: I am not a doctor, so I can't discuss that. You should ask the oncologist.
responses.why: Correct about role, but abrupt; misses the chance to respond to his distress and to help him prepare his questions.

debrief: Good practice: private room, sitting at eye level, time set aside, simple language, information over more than one meeting, ask how much the person wants to know, never criticise their reaction, and say clearly that care will continue. In Indian settings families sometimes ask that the patient not be told; explore this with the family and the patient's own wishes rather than agreeing automatically.
